narrative:
The model determined that you have a 95.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process heavily weighs this predicted outcome, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle—signaled serious academic struggle in law school. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. A score of 26 is well below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, indicating the exam may be a significant barrier for you. Finally, your first-year class rank added further weight in the same direction. Again placing in the bottom decile—compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students—reinforced the pattern of consistently lower performance.

Taken together, these academic signals created a high-confidence prediction that you would not pass the bar on the first try.

You should focus on strengthening the areas within your control. Consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score, seeking academic support or tutoring to improve your class standing if you re-enroll, and exploring schools or programs with additional bar-preparation resources. These steps could meaningfully change your profile for future applications. (248 words)
